* One command at a time: You can only execute one bash command at a time. If you need to run multiple commands sequentially, use `&&` or `;` to chain them together.

### Long-running Commands
* For commands that may run indefinitely, run them in the background and redirect output to a file, e.g. `python3 app.py > server.log 2>&1 &`.

* If a bash command returns exit code `-1`, this means the process hit the soft timeout and is not yet finished. By setting `is_input` to `true`, you can:

  - If you do C-c, you can re-start the process with a longer "timeout" parameter to let it run to completion

### Best Practices
* Directory verification: Before creating new directories or files, first verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
* Directory management: Try to maintain working directory by using absolute paths and avoiding excessive use of `cd`.

### Output Handling
* Output truncation: If the output exceeds a maximum length, it will be truncated before being returned.</description>

    63	Installation via pip
    64	--------------------
    65	
    66	We recommend installation of pyMOR in a [virtual environment](https://virtualenv.pypa.io/en/latest/).
    67	
    68	pyMOR can easily be installed with the [pip](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/)
    69	command:
    70	
    71	    pip install --upgrade pip  # make sure that pip is reasonably new
    72	    pip install pymor[full]
    73	
    74	(Please note that pip must be at least version 9.0.0)
    75	
    76	This will install the latest release of pyMOR on your system with most optional
    77	dependencies.
    78	For Linux we provide binary wheels, so no further system packages should
    79	be required. Use
    80	
    81	    pip install pymor
    82	
    83	for an installation with minimal dependencies.
    84	There are some optional packages not included with `pymor[full]`
    85	because they need additional setup on your system:
    86	
    87	- for support of MPI distributed models and parallelization of greedy algorithms
    88	  (requires MPI development headers and a C compiler):
    89	
    90	      pip install mpi4py
    91	
    92	- dense matrix equation solver for system-theoretic MOR methods, required for
    93	  H-infinity norm calculation (requires OpenBLAS headers and a Fortran
    94	  compiler):
    95	
    96	      pip install slycot
    97	
    98	- dense and sparse matrix equation solver for system-theoretic MOR methods
    99	  (other backends available):
   100	    - from [source](https://gitlab.mpi-magdeburg.mpg.de/mess/cmess-releases)
   101	      (recommended)
   102	    - using a [wheel](https://www.mpi-magdeburg.mpg.de/projects/mess)
   103	
   104	If you are not operating in a virtual environment, you can pass the optional `--user`
   105	argument to pip. pyMOR will then only be installed for your
   106	local user, not requiring administrator privileges.
   107	
   108	To install the latest development version of pyMOR, execute
   109	
   110	    pip install git+https://github.com/pymor/pymor#egg=pymor[full]
   111	
   112	which will require that the [git](https://git-scm.com/) version control system is
   113	installed on your system.
   114	
   115	From time to time, the master branch of pyMOR undergoes major changes and things
   116	might break (this is usually announced on our
   117	[mailing list](http://listserv.uni-muenster.de/mailman/listinfo/pymor-dev)),
   118	so you might prefer to install pyMOR from the current release branch:
   119	
   120	    pip install git+https://github.com/pymor/pymor@2019.2.x#egg=pymor[full]
   121	
   122	Release branches will always stay stable and will only receive bugfix commits
   123	after the corresponding release has been made.

   154	External PDE solvers
   155	--------------------
   156	
   157	pyMOR has been designed with easy integration of external PDE solvers
   158	in mind.
   159	
   160	A basic approach is to use the solver only to generate high-dimensional
   161	system matrices which are then read by pyMOR from disk (`pymor.discretizers.disk`).
   162	Another possibility is to steer the solver via an appropriate network
   163	protocol.
   164	
   165	Whenever possible, we recommend to recompile the solver as a
   166	Python extension module which gives pyMOR direct access to the solver without
   167	any communication overhead. A basic example using
   168	[pybind11](https://github.com/pybind/pybind11) can be found in
   169	`src/pymordemos/minimal_cpp_demo`. Moreover,
   170	we provide bindings for the following solver libraries:
   171	
   172	* [FEniCS](https://fenicsproject.org)
   173	
   174	    MPI-compatible wrapper classes for dolfin linear algebra data structures are
   175	    shipped with pyMOR (`pymor.bindings.fenics`).
   176	    For an example see `pymordemos.thermalbock`, `pymordemos.thermalblock_simple`.
   177	
   178	* [deal.II](https://dealii.org)
   179	
   180	    Python bindings and pyMOR wrapper classes can be found
   181	    [here](https://github.com/pymor/pymor-deal.II).
   182	
   183	* [NGSolve](https://ngsolve.org)
   184	
   185	    Wrapper classes for the NGSolve finite element library are shipped with pyMOR
   186	    (`pymor.bindings.ngsolve`).
   187	    For an example see `pymordemos.thermalblock_simple`.
   188	
   189	
   190	Do not hesitate to contact
   191	[us](http://listserv.uni-muenster.de/mailman/listinfo/pymor-dev) if you
   192	need help with the integration of your PDE solver.
   193	
   194	
   195	External Matrix Equation Solvers
   196	--------------------------------
   197	
   198	pyMOR also provides bindings to matrix equation solvers (in `pymor.bindings`),
   199	which are needed for the system-theoretic methods and need to be installed
   200	separately. Bindings for the following solver libraries are included:
   201	
   202	* [Py-M.E.S.S.](https://www.mpi-magdeburg.mpg.de/projects/mess)
   203	
   204	    The Matrix Equation Sparse Solver library is intended for solving large sparse matrix equations (`pymor.bindings.pymess`).
   205	
   206	* [Slycot](https://github.com/python-control/Slycot)
   207	
   208	    Python wrapper for the Subroutine Library in Systems and Control Theory (SLICOT) is also used for Hardy norm computations (`pymor.bindings.slycot`).
   209

   211	Setting up an Environment for pyMOR Development
   212	-----------------------------------------------
   213	
   214	If you already installed a pyMOR release version, please uninstall it
   215	
   216	    pip uninstall pyMOR
   217	
   218	Then, clone the pyMOR git repository using
   219	
   220	    git clone https://github.com/pymor/pymor $PYMOR_SOURCE_DIR
   221	    cd $PYMOR_SOURCE_DIR
   222	
   223	and, optionally, switch to the branch you are interested in, e.g.
   224	
   225	    git checkout 2019.2.x
   226	
   227	Then, make an editable installation of pyMOR with

   236	simply execute `make test` in the base directory of the pyMOR repository. This

    42	
    43	## Quickstart
    44	
    45	Getting started with CanvasAPI is easy.
    46	
    47	Like most API clients, CanvasAPI exposes a single class that provides access to the rest of the API: `Canvas`.
    48	
    49	The first thing to do is instantiate a new `Canvas` object by providing your Canvas instance’s root API URL and a valid API key:
    50	
    51	```python
    52	# Import the Canvas class
    53	from canvasapi import Canvas
    54	
    55	# Canvas API URL
    56	API_URL = "https://example.com"
    57	# Canvas API key
    58	API_KEY = "p@$$w0rd"
    59	
    60	# Initialize a new Canvas object
    61	canvas = Canvas(API_URL, API_KEY)
    62	```
    63	
    64	You can now use `canvas` to begin making API calls.
    65	
    66	### Working with Canvas Objects
    67	
    68	CanvasAPI converts the JSON responses from the Canvas API into Python objects. These objects provide further access to the Canvas API. You can find a full breakdown of the methods these classes provide in our [class documentation](http://canvasapi.readthedocs.io/en/stable/class-reference.html). Below, you’ll find a few examples of common CanvasAPI use cases.
    69	
    70	#### Course objects
    71	
    72	Courses can be retrieved from the API:
    73	
    74	```python
    75	# Grab course 123456
    76	>>> course = canvas.get_course(123456)
    77	
    78	# Access the course's name
    79	>>> course.name
    80	'Test Course'
    81	
    82	# Update the course's name
    83	>>> course.update(course={'name': 'New Course Name'})
    84	```
    85	
    86	See our documentation on [keyword arguments](#keyword-arguments) for more information about how `course.update()` handles the `name` argument.
    87	
    88	#### User objects
    89	
    90	Individual users can be pulled from the API as well:
    91	
    92	```python
    93	# Grab user 123
    94	>>> user = canvas.get_user(123)
    95	
    96	# Access the user's name
    97	>>> user.name
    98	'Test User'
    99	
   100	# Retrieve a list of courses the user is enrolled in
   101	>>> courses = user.get_courses()
   102	
   103	# Grab a different user by their SIS ID
   104	>>> login_id_user = canvas.get_user('some_user', 'sis_login_id')
   105	```
   106	
   107	#### Paginated Lists
   108	
   109	Some calls, like the `user.get_courses()` call above, will request multiple objects from Canvas’s API. CanvasAPI collects these objects in a `PaginatedList` object. `PaginatedList` generally acts like a regular Python list. You can grab an element by index, iterate over it, and take a slice of it.
   110	
   111	**Warning**: `PaginatedList` lazily loads its elements. Unfortunately, there’s no way to determine the exact number of records Canvas will return without traversing the list fully. This means that `PaginatedList` isn’t aware of its own length and negative indexing is not currently supported.
   112	
   113	Let’s look at how we can use the `PaginatedList` returned by our `get_courses()` call:
   114	
   115	```python
   116	# Retrieve a list of courses the user is enrolled in
   117	>>> courses = user.get_courses()
   118	
   119	>>> print(courses)
   120	<PaginatedList of type Course>
   121	
   122	# Access the first element in our list.
   123	#
   124	# You'll notice the first call takes a moment, but the next N-1
   125	# elements (where N = the per_page argument supplied; the default is 10)
   126	# will be instantly accessible.
   127	>>> print(courses[0])
   128	TST101 Test Course (1234567)
   129	
   130	# Iterate over our course list
   131	>>> for course in courses:
   132	         print(course)
   133	
   134	TST101 Test Course 1 (1234567)
   135	TST102 Test Course 2 (1234568)
   136	TST103 Test Course 3 (1234569)
   137	
   138	# Take a slice of our course list
   139	>>> courses[:2]
   140	[TST101 Test Course 1 (1234567), TST102 Test Course 2 (1234568)]
   141	```

   144	
   145	Most of Canvas’s API endpoints accept a variety of arguments. CanvasAPI allows developers to insert keyword arguments when making calls to endpoints that accept arguments.
   146

   148	# Get all of the active courses a user is currently enrolled in
   149	>>> courses = user.get_courses(enrollment_state='active')
   150	
   151	
   152	# Fetch 50 objects per page when making calls that return a PaginatedList
   153	>>> courses = user.get_courses(per_page=50)
   154	```

    13	### Components
    14	
    15	The fundamental building blocks of Zookeeper are components. The
    16	[`@component`](zookeeper/component.py) decorator is used to turn classes into
    17	components. These component classes can have configurable fields, which are
    18	declared with the `Field` constructor and class-level type annotations. Fields
    19	can be created with or without default values. Components can also be nested,
    20	with `ComponentField`s, such that child componenents can access the field values
    21	defined on their parents.
    22	
    23	For example:
    24	
    25	```python
    26	from zookeeper import component
    27	
    28	@component
    29	class ChildComponent:
    30	    a: int = Field()                          # An `int` field with no default set
    31	    b: str = Field("foo")                     # A `str` field with default value `"foo"`
    32	
    33	@component
    34	class ParentComponent:
    35	    a: int = Field()                          # The same `int` field as the child
    36	    child: ChildComponent = ComponentField()  # A nested component field, of type `ChildComponent`
    37	```
    38	
    39	After instantiation, components can be 'configured' with a configuration
    40	dictionary, containing values for a tree of nested fields. This process
    41	automatically injects the correct values into each field.
    42	
    43	If a child sub-component declares a field which already exists in some
    44	containing ancestor component, then it will pick up the value that's set on the
    45	parent, unless a 'scoped' value is set on the child.
    46	
    47	For example:
    48	
    49	```
    50	from zookeeper import configure
    51	
    52	p = ParentComponent()
    53	
    54	configure(
    55	    p,
    56	    {
    57	        "a": 5,
    58	        "child.a": 4,
    59	    }
    60	)
    61	
    62	>>> 'ChildComponent' is the only concrete component class that satisfies the type
    63	>>> of the annotated parameter 'ParentComponent.child'. Using an instance of this
    64	>>> class by default.
    65	
    66	print(p)
    67

    69	>>>     a = 5,
    70	>>>     child = ChildComponent(
    71	>>>         a = 4,
    72	>>>         b = "foo"
    73	>>>     )
    74	>>> )
    75	```

    78	
    79	The [`@task`](zookeeper/task.py) decorator is used to define Zookeeper tasks and
    80	can be applied to any class that implements an argument-less `run` method. Such
    81	tasks can be run through the Zookeeper CLI, with parameter values passed in
    82	through CLI arguments (`configure` is implicitly called).
    83	
    84	For example:
    85	
    86	```python
    87	from zookeeper import cli, task
    88	
    89	@task
    90	class UseChildA:
    91	    parent: ParentComponent = ComponentField()
    92	    def run(self):
    93	        print(self.parent.child.a)
    94	
    95	@task

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Comprehensive tests for the post-configure hook functionality.
"""

from zookeeper.core.component import component, configure
from zookeeper.core.field import ComponentField, Field


def test_hook_with_no_parameters():
    """Test that hook works with no parameters."""
    calls = []
    
    @component
    class TestComponent:
        a: int = Field(1)
        
        def __component_configured__(self):
            calls.append("called")
    
    comp = TestComponent()
    configure(comp, {})
    assert len(calls) == 1
    print("✓ Test passed: hook with no parameters")


def test_hook_access_to_configured_fields():
    """Test that hook can access configured field values."""
    results = []
    
    @component
    class TestComponent:
        a: int = Field()
        b: str = Field("default")
        
        def __component_configured__(self):
            results.append((self.a, self.b))
    
    comp = TestComponent()
    configure(comp, {"a": 42, "b": "test"})
    assert len(results) == 1
    assert results[0] == (42, "test")
    print("✓ Test passed: hook can access configured fields")


def test_hook_on_components_without_hook():
    """Test that components without hook still work normally."""
    
    @component
    class TestComponent:
        a: int = Field(1)
    
    comp = TestComponent()
    configure(comp, {})  # Should not crash
    assert comp.a == 1
    print("✓ Test passed: components without hook work normally")


def test_hook_exception_handling():
    """Test that exceptions in hook are properly propagated."""
    
    @component
    class TestComponent:
        a: int = Field(1)
        
        def __component_configured__(self):
            raise ValueError("Hook error")
    
    comp = TestComponent()
    try:
        configure(comp, {})
        assert False, "Should have raised ValueError"
    except ValueError as e:
        assert str(e) == "Hook error"
    print("✓ Test passed: hook exceptions are propagated")


def test_nested_hooks_execution_order():
    """Test that nested component hooks are called in correct order."""
    execution_order = []
    
    @component
    class GrandChild:
        x: int = Field()
        def __component_configured__(self):
            execution_order.append(f"grandchild_{self.x}")
    
    @component
    class Child:
        gc: GrandChild = ComponentField()
        y: int = Field()
        def __component_configured__(self):
            execution_order.append(f"child_{self.y}")
            
    @component
    class Parent:
        c: Child = ComponentField()
        z: int = Field()
        def __component_configured__(self):
            execution_order.append(f"parent_{self.z}")
    
    parent = Parent()
    configure(parent, {"z": 1, "c.y": 2, "c.gc.x": 3})
    
    # The deepest nested components should be configured first
    assert execution_order == ["grandchild_3", "child_2", "parent_1"]
    print("✓ Test passed: nested hooks called in correct order")


def test_hook_called_only_once():
    """Test that hook is called exactly once even for complex configurations."""
    call_count = 0
    
    @component
    class TestComponent:
        a: int = Field()
        def __component_configured__(self):
            nonlocal call_count
            call_count += 1
    
    comp = TestComponent()
    configure(comp, {"a": 1})
    assert call_count == 1
    
    # Try to configure again - should fail but not call hook again
    try:
        configure(comp, {"a": 2})
        assert False, "Should not be able to configure twice"
    except ValueError:
        pass
    
    assert call_count == 1
    print("✓ Test passed: hook called only once")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Running comprehensive hook tests...")
    
    test_hook_with_no_parameters()
    test_hook_access_to_configured_fields()
    test_hook_on_components_without_hook()
    test_hook_exception_handling()
    test_nested_hooks_execution_order()
    test_hook_called_only_once()
    
    print("All comprehensive tests passed!")

def test_inherited_hook():
    """Test that child classes inherit the hook."""
    calls = []
    
    @component
    class Parent:
        a: int = Field()
        
        def __component_configured__(self):
            calls.append(f"parent_{self.a}")
    
    @component
    class Child(Parent):
        b: str = Field("default")
        # Child inherits __component_configured__ from Parent

    configure(child, {"a": 1, "b": "test"})
    assert len(calls) == 1
    assert calls[0] == "parent_1"
    print("✓ Test passed: inherited hook works")


def test_overridden_hook():
    """Test that child classes can override the hook."""
    calls = []
    
    @component
    class Parent:
        a: int = Field()
        
        def __component_configured__(self):
            calls.append(f"parent_{self.a}")
    
    @component
    class Child(Parent):
        b: str = Field("default")
        
        def __component_configured__(self):  # Override parent hook
            calls.append(f"child_{self.a}_{self.b}")
    
    child = Child()
    configure(child, {"a": 1, "b": "test"})
    assert len(calls) == 1
    assert calls[0] == "child_1_test"
    print("✓ Test passed: overridden hook works")


def test_hook_with_super_call():
    """Test that hooks can call super()."""
    calls = []
    
    @component
    class Parent:
        a: int = Field()
        
        def __component_configured__(self):
            calls.append(f"parent_{self.a}")

        b: str = Field("default")
        
        def __component_configured__(self):  # Override and call super
            super().__component_configured__()
            calls.append(f"child_{self.b}")

    assert len(calls) == 2
    assert calls[0] == "parent_1"
    assert calls[1] == "child_test"
    print("✓ Test passed: hook with super() call works")

    print("Running inheritance tests...")
    
    test_inherited_hook()
    test_overridden_hook()

### 8.2 Implementation Summary

My implementation adds a post-configure hook mechanism:

1. **During component decoration** (`@component`):
   - Checks if the class defines a `__component_configured__` method
   - If found, saves it as `__component_configured_hook__` on the class
   - Sets `__component_configured__` to `False` (the boolean flag)

2. **During configuration** (`configure()`):
   - After all configuration is complete and `instance.__component_configured__ = True` is set
   - Checks if the instance has `__component_configured_hook__`
   - If found, calls the hook method

### 8.3 Key Features

- ✅ **Optional**: Components don't need to implement the hook
- ✅ **Nested Support**: Hooks are called for nested components in the correct order (deepest first)
- ✅ **Error Propagation**: Exceptions in hooks are properly propagated
- ✅ **Inheritance Support**: Child classes can inherit or override hooks
- ✅ **Access to Configured Values**: Hooks can access fully configured field values
- ✅ **Called Exactly Once**: Each component's hook is called exactly once during configuration

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Demonstration of the new post-configure hook feature.
This replaces the old validate_configuration functionality.
"""

from zookeeper.core.component import component, configure
from zookeeper.core.field import ComponentField, Field

print("=== Zookeeper Post-Configure Hook Demo ===\n")

# Example 1: Basic hook usage
print("1. Basic hook usage:")

@component
class DatabaseConfig:
    host: str = Field()
    port: int = Field(5432)
    
    def __component_configured__(self):
        # This method is called after configuration is complete
        print(f"   Database configured: {self.host}:{self.port}")
        # Could perform validation here
        if self.port <= 0 or self.port > 65535:
            raise ValueError("Invalid port number")

db = DatabaseConfig()
configure(db, {"host": "localhost", "port": 3306})
print(f"   Result: host={db.host}, port={db.port}\n")


# Example 2: Nested components with hooks
print("2. Nested components with hooks:")

@component
class AppConfig:
    name: str = Field("MyApp")
    debug: bool = Field(False)
    
    def __component_configured__(self):
        print(f"   App '{self.name}' configured (debug={self.debug})")

@component
class WebServer:
    app: AppConfig = ComponentField()
    port: int = Field(8080)
    
    def __component_configured__(self):
        print(f"   Web server configured on port {self.port}")

server = WebServer()
configure(server, {
    "port": 8000,
    "app.name": "DemoApp", 
    "app.debug": True
})
print(f"   Result: server_port={server.port}, app_name={server.app.name}\n")


# Example 3: Components without hooks still work normally
print("3. Components without hooks:")

@component
class SimpleConfig:
    value: int = Field(42)

simple = SimpleConfig()
configure(simple, {"value": 100})
print(f"   Simple config works: value={simple.value}")
print("   (No hook defined, so nothing extra happened)\n")

print("=== Demo Complete ===")
print("The __component_configured__ hook provides a clean way to perform")
print("validation or initialization after configuration, replacing the")
print("previous validate_configuration mechanism.")
</parameter>
